message.content:
You are an adversarial deep-tech investor. MARKET skeptic: is the customer and budget real? Would anyone pay in the next 18 months? Attack TAM inflation.
Default to skepticism; score 1-10 where 7+ means you would actually take a meeting. Thesis:
{
  "name": "Kelvin Light (athermal high-efficiency multi-wavelength laser source)",
  "one_liner": "The bold bet: kill the TEC — an uncooled, high-power, multi-wavelength external laser source that attacks the single largest power and reliability sink in every optical link.",
  "wedge": "An ELSFP-form-factor external laser module built around uncooled/athermal multi-wavelength emission (quantum-dot gain, which tolerates 80°C uncooled operation, and/or comb generation) plus zero-static-power wavelength stabilization (photoconductive/PCM-assisted locking instead of brute-force thermoelectric cooling). Target spec: cut ELS wall-plug power 40-60% versus today's DFB+TEC modules at the ~24.5dBm launch powers CPO links require. Sold into the standardized socket the OIF ELSFP and OCI MSA just guaranteed — first customers are CPO switch/system builders (Broadcom ecosystem partners, Celestial/Marvell-class XPU programs) and the hyperscalers who wrote the standards.",
  "why_now": "The pain is quantified and public: Meta says ~90% of optical link failures trace to lasers and lasers consume ~60% of link power; lasers+TECs are ~70% of ELS power draw. NVIDIA just paid $4B into Coherent/Lumentum purely for laser supply security — the demand side is desperate. The socket is standardized (ELSFP-02.0, Jan 2025; OCI MSA WDM, Mar 2026), so a component startup doesn't need to win an architecture war. The enabling pieces matured independently: QD-on-Si epi supply chains exist (Quintessent/IQE), Tower/OpenLight offer open-foundry gain integration, comb sources are productizing (Xscape FalconX 8λ), and heaterless ring locking was demonstrated (NewPhotonics). Nobody has assembled 'uncooled + multi-λ + high power + ELSFP' into one module — every light-source startup is attacking a different sub-problem.",
  "market": "Lasers/light sources are the largest BOM and power line item in a CPO market going from $46M (2024) to $8-10B (2030), plus the pluggable market (~$26B datacom optics in 2026) where LPO's power story makes efficient lasers equally valuable. If ELS modules are 15-25% of CPO system value, the light-source TAM is $1.5-2.5B by 2030; a startup with a differentiated module taking 10-15% share is a $200-400M revenue business — and the NVIDIA/Coherent/Lumentum dynamic shows laser suppliers now command strategic (not component) valuations.",
  "competition": "The most crowded deep-tech lane in the sector, be clear-eyed: Coherent and Lumentum (now NVIDIA-capitalized with purchase commitments — they own today's sockets); the funded startup cohort each holding one piece — Xscape (combs, $81M, Cisco+NVIDIA backing), OpenLight (integrated InP, $84M), Scintil ($58M, NVIDIA), Quintessent (QD, Tower), Aylight (ETH, multiwavelength); Broadcom's internal ELS. Your differentiation must be the system-level power number (module wall-plug efficiency at spec launch power, uncooled), not a device physics claim — if you can't beat Lumentum's next-gen module by >30% in qualified testing, this company shouldn't exist.",
  "moat": "Hard-won physics and reliability data: uncooled high-power operation with telecom-grade wavelength stability is a genuine multi-year materials/photonics problem (QD gain dynamics, athermal cavity design, locking electronics), and the resulting qualification corpus (HTOL hours, FIT rates — Intel's 0.09 FIT benchmark is the bar) is the true barrier; hyperscalers qualify lasers over years and don't switch casually. Patents on the athermal stabilization architecture matter here more than in software theses. Post-qualification, laser sockets are among the stickiest in hardware.",
  "capital_intensity": "High and unavoidable — this is the deep-tech play: III-V epi runs, hybrid integration development, reliability labs (burn-in racks, HTOL chambers), and 3-4 module generations. ~$15-20M seed/A to a working prototype module (leveraging Tower/OpenLight and IQE-style epi supply rather than owning a fab), $80-150M cumulative through hyperscaler qualification and early production. Comparable trajectory: Xscape at $81M pre-production. Non-negotiable: an NVIDIA/Cisco/hyperscaler strategic in the round, both for validation and for the qualification fast-path.",
  "software_mvp": "This week (genuinely useful, not decoration): a laser reliability and link-power modeling platform — physics-based FIT-rate and wavelength-drift models fit to published data (Intel's 45,000-hour HTOL corpus, Meta's failure statistics), plus an ELS power-budget optimizer that shows hyperscalers exactly what an uncooled architecture saves across a 100K-GPU fabric. It sharpens your own spec targets, generates design-partner conversations a year before hardware exists, and its telemetry/health-prediction module becomes the firmware companion product (laser fleet monitoring) once modules ship.",
  "risks": [
    "Physics failure mode: uncooled operation may not reach the power+linewidth+stability corner CPO needs; QD output power per wavelength remains the known weakness",
    "Reliability qualification takes 2-3 years of accumulated hours no amount of money compresses — the market may lock in Lumentum/Coherent sockets first, especially with NVIDIA's purchase commitments steering volume",
    "Crowded cap tables: five funded startups plus two NVIDIA-backed incumbents means acquirer supply may exhaust before your exit window",
    "InP/GaAs epi supply chain concentration (China exposure on InP substrates) adds geopolitical input risk",
    "Capital markets risk: this needs $100M+ across a window where photonics funding is hostage to the AI capex cycle; a 2027 AI-spending pause strands the company mid-qualification",
    "Team risk: requires world-class III-V materials + photonics + reliability engineering simultaneously — perhaps 200 people on earth qualify, mostly at Intel/Lumentum/UCSB"
  ]
}

Use this skill whenever the developer asks which Slack API method does something, needs a method's required OAuth scopes or token type, wants to call or test a Web API method, is handling cursor pagination (next_cursor), hitting rate limits (tier/ratelimited/Retry-After), or debugging API errors like missing_scope, invalid_auth, or channel_not_found. Also trigger when they paste a slack.com/api/ URL or a docs.slack.dev/reference/methods link, or ask how to list/fetch/post/update Slack resources via the API. Use whenever the developer wants to log in, add a team, switch workspaces, or authenticate with Slack; whenever Slack CLI commands are needed (local development with `slack run`, managing app lifecycle, the manifest); or when searching the Slack developer documentation for any topic (socket mode, the Events API, OAuth, manifests, Bolt).

- slack:slack-search: Guidance for effectively searching Slack to find messages, files, channels, and people
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

input.rationale: The pain point is real, quantified, and public (lasers dominate link power and failures; power is the binding constraint in AI datacenters), and socket standardization (ELSFP) genuinely de-risks the architecture question. But the market structure is hostile to a new merchant entrant: the two largest ELS sockets are already foreclosed (Broadcom self-supplies; NVIDIA prepaid ~$4B to Coherent/Lumentum to lock capacity — the thesis cites this as demand validation when it is actually addressable-market removal), leaving 3-5 real buyers of unproven volume. There is no credible paying customer inside 18 months: laser procurement selects on accumulated HTOL/FIT data a startup cannot have for 2-3 years, and the Meta failure stat the thesis leans on makes buyers MORE conservative about unproven laser vendors, not less. The TAM stacks three optimistic ratios (top-of-range $8-10B 2030 CPO forecast extrapolated from $46M actuals × 15-25% ELS value share that will compress under hyperscaler commoditization × 10-15% share for a company unqualified before ~2029), and first revenue lands exactly at the edge of the forecast window and possibly past the AI capex cycle. "Kill the TEC" is also less novel than framed — uncooled DFBs have shipped in CWDM4/DR/FR for a decade; the unproven part is uncooled + DWDM-grade stability + 24.5dBm simultaneously, which the thesis's own risk list flags as the known physics weakness. The strategic-acquisition exit path (laser suppliers now command strategic valuations) is the strongest market argument and keeps this from scoring lower, but the thesis itself concedes acquirer supply may exhaust before the exit window. Below meeting threshold as constructed, though a hyperscaler LOI or incumbent-as-customer reframing would flip it.
fatal_flaws: No revenue path inside 18 months: the only near-term dollars are NRE/design-partnership money; ELS purchase decisions require 2-3 years of per-customer qualification, and the proposed software MVP (FIT/link-power modeling) has no budget owner at any hyperscaler — nobody pays for reliability models from a vendor with zero reliability data.

Merchant-addressable TAM is 5-10x smaller than claimed: Broadcom self-supplies its ELS and NVIDIA's $4B prepayment locks Coherent/Lumentum capacity, removing the two largest socket pools; the thesis cites this deal as demand validation when it is actually the addressable market being foreclosed. What remains is 3-5 buyers of unproven volume, and a standardized socket does not create a merchant market when qualification is bespoke per customer.

TAM built on three stacked optimistic ratios: aggressive end of 2030 CPO forecasts extrapolated from $46M of 2024 actuals, times an ELS value share (15-25%) that hyperscalers will compress exactly as they commoditized DFBs and DSPs, times 10-15% share for a company that cannot complete qualification before ~2029.

The cited pain cuts against the startup: 90% of failures being lasers makes buyers maximally conservative on laser sourcing — they buy accumulated HTOL hours and FIT rates (Intel's 0.09 FIT bar), which no amount of capital compresses; vendor lists for the 2027-2028 CPO ramp are being written now, before the company can exist as a qualified supplier.

Timing/capital mismatch: $80-150M consumed before first qualified revenue at ~2029-2030, the exact edge of the forecast window, with the entire demand signal riding one cycle (AI capex); a 2027 pause strands the company mid-qualification with no fallback market.
improvements: Rebuild the TAM bottoms-up from actual sockets: enumerate which CPO/XPU programs buy third-party external ELS versus self-supply or locked suppliers, and count units and ASPs per program rather than percent-of-system-value ratios.
Get a paid design win before hardware: a hyperscaler or XPU-program JDA/LOI with explicit power-and-FIT spec gates is the only market evidence that matters; the round should be contingent on one.

Reframe the wedge to fastest-to-revenue: sell the uncooled QD gain chip or the zero-static-power stabilization subsystem TO Lumentum/Coherent/Broadcom (incumbents as customers, not competitors) — that creates 18-24 month revenue and rides their qualification corpus instead of rebuilding it.
Reposition the software MVP honestly as BD tooling and spec-sharpening, not a product line; claiming it as a revenue wedge weakens credibility with anyone who has sold to hyperscalers.

Pressure-test the 40-60% power claim against Lumentum/Coherent next-gen module roadmaps and translate it into dollars-per-port TCO for a 100K-GPU fabric to establish whether buyers pay a premium for it or simply demand it at parity pricing.

Model the downside scenarios that shrink ELS attach: LPO displacing CPO at some tiers, and integrated per-lane lasers (OpenLight-style heterogeneous InP) eliminating the external laser socket entirely.
